passage:
"Farida, sorry, where do I click to filter the sheet?"
"I showed you yesterday." Farida sighed and reached for the mouse. "Top row. Data. Filter. It's not hard."
"Okay. And then the sort?"
"Same thing. Honestly."
"Right. Yes. Got it."
Damini nodded at the screen, though the menu had already gone. She did not ask again. In the evening she copied the numbers by hand into a new sheet, which took two hours, and hoped nobody would ask why.
"All good?" Farida called, packing up.
"All good."
On the way home Damini thought: everyone else seems to understand, and she had not wanted to be the slow one.

qa.q: How long did Damini take copying the numbers by hand?
qa.a: Copying the numbers by hand took two hours.

qa.q: Why did Damini say "Got it" when she had not understood?
qa.a: Damini felt slow and embarrassed after Farida's sigh and did not want to be the slow one.

qa.q: What could Damini do next to actually learn the filter?
qa.a: Ask for a short, slow demo when Farida is not in a hurry, or write the steps down and repeat them back.

qa.q: How might Farida see the exchange?
qa.a: Farida probably thinks the task is simple and does not realise the sigh made Damini stop asking, so Farida believes all is good.

grounding: Shows a learner pretending to follow an impatient expert and quietly stopping questions.

passage: Looking back, my first month at the design studio taught me more about teaching than about design. Parveen, the senior who had to show me the software, spoke fast and sighed when I asked anything twice. "Just use the layers, it's obvious." After the third sigh I stopped asking. I nodded, wrote nothing, and stayed late redoing files I had misunderstood. What I remember most is the heat in my face. I was not stupid. I just needed the first step slowly. When Parveen was away for a week, a colleague showed me the same tool in ten minutes without any hurry, and it clicked. It was never the tool. It was the tone. - Madhav

qa.q: What did Parveen say about the layers?
qa.a: Parveen said, "Just use the layers, it's obvious."

qa.q: What was Madhav feeling after the third sigh?
qa.a: Ashamed and slow, with heat in the face, so Madhav stopped asking.

qa.q: What small step could Madhav take with a hurried teacher next time?
qa.a: Ask for the first step to be shown slowly just once, or write the steps down and repeat them back.

qa.q: How might Parveen have seen the situation?
qa.a: Parveen probably thought the software was simple to explain and did not realise the sighing made Madhav stop asking.

grounding: Shows a learner made to feel slow by an impatient expert's tone, who then stops asking questions.

passage:
Chinmay, you're scared to ask your seniors things? Let your Samir uncle tell you about my first year at the tool factory.
They put me under a machinist called Bhosale. Brilliant hands. But every time I asked a question, he sighed like I had insulted him. "I already told you. Are you slow?" After the third sigh I stopped asking. I nodded. I said, "Yes, got it," when I hadn't got anything.
One morning I set the lathe speed wrong because I was too scared to check. A whole batch of parts was ruined. I thought I'd be sent home.
Instead the foreman, old Joshi-ji, sat me down with a cup of tea and said, "Show me what you think you're doing." I showed him. He didn't laugh once. In one hour with him I learned more than in three months with Bhosale.
It wasn't that the lathe was hard, beta. It was that I was afraid to ask.

qa.q: What was the name of the machinist Samir worked under?
qa.a: A machinist called Bhosale.

qa.q: What was young Samir feeling after the third sigh?
qa.a: Samir felt slow and humiliated, so frightened of the contempt that he stopped asking and pretended to understand.

qa.q: What choice by Joshi-ji turned things around in the story?
qa.a: Joshi-ji sat down with tea, asked Samir to show what he thought he was doing and did not laugh, which made it safe to learn.

qa.q: How might Bhosale have seen the ruined batch?
qa.a: Bhosale might blame the young worker as careless, not seeing that his sighs had made Samir too scared to check.

grounding: An elder recalls learning from an impatient expert whose contempt made him stop asking, and a patient teacher who reopened his mind.

passage:
Arohi had one hour before her leave started, and she had to teach Sabina the clinic's billing software before she went.
She clicked fast. "Patient ID, here. Then this tab, then the insurance code, obviously. Then you close the batch." Sabina asked where the insurance code came from. Arohi sighed. "From the card. It's written on the card." Her tone said: everyone knows that.
Sabina felt her cheeks go warm. The next time she didn't understand, she didn't ask. She wrote "?" in her notebook and nodded. By the end of the hour her page had seven question marks.
"All clear?" Arohi said, grabbing her bag.
"All clear," said Sabina.
The next morning the first patient's bill wouldn't close. Sabina stared at the screen for twenty minutes before a nurse from the next desk showed her a button Arohi had never mentioned. She felt stupid, though the software was not really that hard.

qa.q: How many question marks were on Sabina's page by the end of the hour?
qa.a: Her page had seven question marks.

qa.q: Why did Sabina stop asking questions?
qa.a: Sabina felt embarrassed and slow after Arohi's sigh and tone, so asking again felt too humiliating.

qa.q: What could Arohi have done differently, even with only an hour?
qa.a: Arohi could have answered patiently and asked Sabina to try one bill while watching, so the gaps showed up before she left.

qa.q: How might Arohi have felt as she left?
qa.a: Arohi was probably rushed and distracted, thinking about her leave, and believed the handover was done.

grounding: Shows a learner taught by an impatient expert who stops asking and pretends to follow, then struggles alone.

passage:
In the design studio in Bandra, Gurpreet was learning the layout software from Farida, the senior designer. On day one he asked how to lock a layer. Farida rolled her eyes and said, "Seriously? That's first-week stuff." The two interns at the next desk smiled.
After that, Gurpreet stopped asking. When Farida showed him shortcuts, he nodded and said, "Yes, yes." At night he stayed back alone, watching tutorial videos with the sound low, trying to find what she had skipped.
By the second week he was tired and jumpy. He had started to believe he was too slow for the job. When he finally sent a draft, it had three layers on the wrong setting. Farida marked them in red without a word.
In the lift, the office manager asked how he was finding the work. Gurpreet said, "Fine," and looked at the floor numbers.

qa.q: What did Gurpreet ask about on day one?
qa.a: He asked how to lock a layer.

qa.q: How did Gurpreet feel by the second week?
qa.a: Gurpreet felt tired, jumpy and slow, beginning to believe he was not good enough for the job.

qa.q: What could help Gurpreet get unstuck?
qa.a: Gurpreet could ask the office manager or another colleague for a patient walk-through, and say honestly that the eye-rolls made asking hard.

qa.q: How might the interns' smiles have felt to Gurpreet?
qa.a: The smiles probably made Gurpreet feel mocked and exposed, adding to the shame of Farida's comment.

grounding: Illustrates a learner whose teacher's contempt makes him stop asking and pretend to follow, losing confidence.

passage:
"Pivot table. Rows, values, filter. Got it?" Maria's cursor was already moving.
"Sorry, which column goes in rows?"
Maria sighed. "Region, Suraj. I showed you this yesterday."
"Right. Yes."
"And sales go in values. Obviously."
Suraj nodded. He had no idea why his totals kept looking wrong.
"Any questions?"
He had three. "No, it's clear."
"Good. Regional sheet by four."
At four he sent it. Ten minutes later a message came: "You've counted instead of summed. Did you listen at all?"
"I'll fix it," he typed.
At his desk he searched a video site for "pivot table basics" and watched with the sound at the lowest setting, angling the screen away from the aisle.
Across the aisle, Nikhil leaned over. "She talks to everyone like that. Ask me next time, no sighing, promise."
Suraj gave a small, tired laugh. "Okay. Thanks."

qa.q: What mistake did Maria find in Suraj's sheet?
qa.a: He had counted instead of summed.

qa.q: Why did Suraj say "No, it's clear" when he had three questions?
qa.a: Suraj felt slow and embarrassed after Maria's sighs and her "Obviously", so he was afraid another question would bring more scorn.

qa.q: How could Maria explain the next task so Suraj keeps asking?
qa.a: She could slow down, say why each column goes where it does, and invite questions without sighing, perhaps letting him build one step while she watches.

qa.q: How does Nikhil see what is happening to Suraj?
qa.a: Nikhil sees it as Maria's habit, not Suraj's failing, and offers to be someone Suraj can ask without being made to feel stupid.

grounding: Shows a learner taught with contempt by an impatient expert who stops asking questions and pretends to follow.
